lessons.title: Who Am I Today?
objectives: Pretend to be a character using voice and body
Change voice to show different characters
explanation: In drama, we pretend to be someone or something else. This someone is called a character.
We can change our voice to show different characters: a big, deep voice for a giant; a tiny, squeaky voice for a mouse; a slow, creaky voice for an old tortoise.
We also use our faces and bodies: a giant stomps and stands tall, a mouse scurries and peeks. Acting is playing with care, so that others can understand our pretend.

lessons.title: My First Puppet Show
objectives: Make a simple puppet

prerequisites: Can pretend to be a character
explanation: A puppet is a figure that is moved by a person, called a puppeteer. Puppets can be made from socks, paper bags, sticks or wood.
To make a puppet talk, open and close its mouth (or move it a little) when it speaks. Look at the puppet, not the audience, so the audience watches the puppet too.
India has famous puppet traditions, like the colourful Kathputli string puppets of Rajasthan. Puppets have entertained people for many hundreds of years.

lessons.title: Silent Stories
objectives: Mime everyday actions clearly
Create a freeze frame showing a story moment
prerequisites: Can pretend with voice and body
explanation: Mime is acting without words. A mime artist shows actions using only face and body — like pretending to climb a ladder or open a heavy door.
Good mime is clear and detailed: if you pretend to hold a cup, keep your hand the same shape the whole time!
A freeze frame (or tableau) is like a photograph: actors freeze still to show an important moment in a story. The audience can guess what is happening from the bodies and faces.

The children shouted, "There's a door!" He found it, stepped out and bowed. Nobody had said a word — but everyone had understood.

lessons.title: Let's Put on a Play
objectives: Act out a familiar story in a group with roles

prerequisites: Can mime and make freeze frames
explanation: A play is a story acted out for an audience. Each actor has a role — the character they play.
A play has a beginning (meet the characters), a middle (a problem happens) and an end (the problem is solved). Actors need to remember what happens next and listen to each other.
The audience has a job too: watch quietly, laugh at funny parts and clap at the end. Actors wait for laughter before speaking again!

lessons.title: Yes, And!
objectives: Improvise a scene by accepting and building on offers
Use status to create interesting characters
explanation: Improvisation (improv) is acting without a script — making it up as you go. The golden rule is "Yes, and…": accept what your partner offers and add something new.
If your partner says, "Captain, the ship is sinking!", don't say "No, it isn't." Say, "Yes, and the sharks are circling — grab the bucket!"

Status is how powerful or confident a character seems. A king has high status; a nervous servant has low status. Playing with status — like a servant who secretly runs the palace — makes scenes interesting.

vocabulary.meaning: acting without a script

examples: "Yes, and" turning a picnic into an alien adventure.

story.text: In drama club, Zuri said, "Look, a dragon!" Kiko said, "No, it's just a cloud." The scene died. They tried again. "Look, a dragon!" "Yes, and it's carrying a letter for you!" Suddenly the scene took off — they were reading a dragon's invitation to a party on the Moon.

lessons.title: Theatre of the People
objectives: Match Indian folk theatre forms to their regions
Compare India's puppet traditions
explanation: India has many folk theatre forms, often performed outdoors at festivals with music and dance. Tamasha from Maharashtra blends song, dance (especially Lavani) and comedy. Yakshagana from coastal Karnataka performs epic stories with grand costumes and headgear.
Jatra from Bengal and Odisha is travelling theatre with dramatic stories; Nautanki from Uttar Pradesh mixes music and melodrama; Bhavai is from Gujarat.
India's puppet traditions include Kathputli string puppets (Rajasthan), Tholu Bommalata leather shadow puppets (Andhra Pradesh), Bommalattam (Tamil Nadu), and Putul Nach rod puppets (West Bengal).

story.text: In an Andhra village, Ivaan sat in the dark before a white cloth screen lit by a lamp. Colourful leather figures of Rama and Hanuman pressed against it, glowing like stained glass. The puppeteers sang, drummed and moved the figures all at once. "Shadows can tell stories too," Ivaan whispered.

lessons.title: Writing a Scene
objectives: Write a short scene in script format
Create conflict and subtext in dialogue
explanation: A script shows the character's name, then their words (dialogue). Stage directions, usually in brackets or italics, tell actors what to do: (She slams the door.)
Good drama needs conflict — characters wanting different things, or a character facing an obstacle. Without conflict, nothing happens!
Subtext is what a character really means underneath their words. If someone says "I'm fine" while slamming a door, the subtext is that they are not fine.

story.title: The Last Mango
story.text: Zuri wrote a scene: two siblings, one mango. "You have it," said the brother, sighing loudly. "No, YOU have it," said the sister, staring at it. Neither moved. The audience laughed — they could see both secretly wanted it. "That's subtext," her teacher said. "What they say isn't what they mean."

lessons.title: The Theatre Team
objectives: Name stage areas and theatre roles
Design simple set, lighting and costume ideas
explanation: Stage directions use stage areas from the actor's point of view facing the audience: upstage (back), downstage (front), stage left and stage right. Upstage is called that because old stages sloped upwards at the back.
A play needs a whole team: the director (guides the actors and vision), stage manager (runs the show), and designers for set, lighting, sound and costume.
Design helps tell the story: blue light can suggest night or sadness; a single chair can suggest a whole palace; a costume can show a character's age and personality.

lessons.title: Kalidasa and Sophocles
objectives: Describe the features of Sanskrit and Greek drama
Compare their aims and conventions
explanation: Sanskrit drama follows principles from the Natya Shastra and aims to evoke rasa in the audience. Plays often end happily. Kalidasa, commonly placed around the 4th–5th century CE, wrote "Abhijnanashakuntalam" (The Recognition of Shakuntala). Its English translation by William Jones in 1789 impressed European writers such as Goethe.

Greek drama arose in Athens in the 5th century BCE, performed at festivals for Dionysus in open-air theatres. Tragedies by Aeschylus, Sophocles and Euripides showed heroes facing fate; a chorus commented on the action. Aristophanes wrote comedies mocking politicians.
Aristotle's "Poetics" said tragedy produces catharsis — a release of pity and fear. Both traditions developed sophisticated theories about how drama affects audiences.

vocabulary.meaning: a drama in which the hero suffers downfall
a group commenting on the action in Greek drama
an emotional release

examples: Shakuntala's ring and the curse of forgetting.

story.title: A Ring in a Fish
story.text: In Kalidasa's play, King Dushyanta forgets his wife Shakuntala because of a sage's curse. Only the ring he gave her can restore his memory — but she loses it in a river. Much later, a fisherman finds it inside a fish. The king remembers everything, and after more trials, the family is reunited.

lessons.title: All the World's a Stage
objectives: Describe Shakespeare's theatre and major plays
Analyse a soliloquy for meaning and performance
explanation: William Shakespeare (1564–1616) wrote about 37 plays, including tragedies (Hamlet, Macbeth), comedies (A Midsummer Night's Dream) and histories. Many were performed at the Globe Theatre in London, where poorer audience members stood in the yard as "groundlings".

Shakespeare often wrote in iambic pentameter — lines of ten syllables with a da-DUM rhythm. A soliloquy is a speech in which a character speaks their thoughts alone, such as Hamlet's "To be, or not to be".

Shakespeare has a rich life in India: Parsi theatre staged adaptations in the 19th century, and films such as Vishal Bhardwaj's "Maqbool" (Macbeth), "Omkara" (Othello) and "Haider" (Hamlet) reimagined the plays in Indian settings.

story.title: The Groundlings' Theatre
story.text: In 1600, a penny bought you a standing place in the Globe's yard. The groundlings cheered heroes, booed villains and threw nutshells. On a bare stage with few props, Shakespeare's words had to paint the scenes: "this wooden O", as one play calls the theatre, became battlefields, forests and palaces.

lessons.title: Voices of Modern Indian Theatre
objectives: Analyse major works of modern Indian playwrights
Explain how they used myth, folk forms and politics
explanation: After independence, Indian theatre flourished in many languages. Marathi playwright Vijay Tendulkar wrote "Ghashiram Kotwal" (1972), using Dashavatar and folk forms to explore power, and "Shantata! Court Chalu Aahe" (Silence! The Court Is in Session). Some of his plays faced censorship and protests.

Girish Karnad (Kannada) reworked myths and history in "Hayavadana", "Tughlaq" and "Nagamandala", using folk theatre conventions like Yakshagana. Habib Tanvir's Naya Theatre worked with Chhattisgarhi folk performers, as in "Charandas Chor".
Badal Sircar (Bengali) developed "Third Theatre" — low-cost performances in open spaces, close to the audience. The National School of Drama, founded in 1959, trained generations of theatre artists.

vocabulary.meaning: a person who writes plays

examples: "Ghashiram Kotwal" in Pune's Peshwa era.

story.title: The Play That Toured the World
story.text: When "Ghashiram Kotwal" premiered in 1972, its portrayal of the Peshwa era provoked protests in Pune. Yet its brilliant use of song, dance and a human wall of chorus actors made it a landmark. The production went on to tour Europe, showing how a Marathi play could speak to the world about power and corruption.

lessons.title: Theatre That Changes Things
objectives: Develop a director's concept for a scene
Evaluate street theatre and forum theatre as tools for change
explanation: A director develops a concept — a unifying idea about what the production means and how it will look and feel — then guides actors, designers and rehearsals towards it.

Street theatre takes performance to public spaces to raise awareness. Safdar Hashmi's group Jana Natya Manch (Janam), founded in 1973, performed plays on workers' rights; Hashmi was fatally attacked during a performance in 1989, and his colleagues returned to finish the play two days later.

Brazilian director Augusto Boal created the Theatre of the Oppressed, including forum theatre, in which audience members ("spect-actors") stop a scene and step in to try different solutions to a problem. Such methods are used worldwide in education and community work.

examples: A street play on clean water in a market.

story.title: Halla Bol
story.text: On 1 January 1989, Safdar Hashmi's troupe was performing the street play "Halla Bol" near Delhi when they were attacked; Hashmi died the next day. Two days later, his wife Moloyashree Hashmi and the troupe returned to the same spot and completed the performance before a large crowd — a powerful statement about art and courage.
